content: Drug addiction is a chronic and relapsing condition. Primary prevention efforts should focus on reducing the likelihood of initial drug use or preventing the progression from experimental use to addiction. Schools are an ideal setting for implementing preventive interventions aimed at addressing these issues. The objective of this review was to assess the effectiveness of universal school-based interventions in reducing illicit drug use compared to standard school curricula or the absence of any intervention. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group's Trials Register, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, PubMed, and EMBASE, covering studies up to September 2013. Researchers in the field were also contacted, and reference lists of relevant articles were reviewed. The review included 51 randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving a total of 127,146 participants. Most of the interventions were delivered to students in the sixth and seventh grades, with the majority of studies conducted in the United States. The interventions were categorized into three main approaches: social competence, social influence, and combined approaches. Social Competence Approach Marijuana use within 12 months of follow-up: The social competence approach showed a trend toward reduced marijuana use compared to usual curricula or no intervention (risk ratio [RR] 0.90; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.81 to 1.01, based on four studies with 9,456 participants, moderate-quality evidence). Seven additional studies assessed this outcome but were not included in the meta-analysis. Of these, two studies demonstrated a significant positive effect of the intervention, three showed no significant effect, one favored the control group, and one showed a trend favoring the control group. Marijuana use at 12 months or longer: The intervention demonstrated a protective effect (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.74 to 1.00, based on one study with 2,678 participants, high-quality evidence). Seven other studies assessed this outcome without providing data for meta-analysis. Two studies showed significant positive effects, three showed no significant effect, one favored the control group, and one showed a trend favoring the control group. Hard drug use within 12 months: No significant difference was observed (RR 0.69; 95% CI 0.40 to 1.18, based on one study with 2,090 participants, moderate-quality evidence). Two additional studies assessed this outcome without meta-analytic data. One study found comparable results between the intervention and control groups, while the other showed a non-significant trend favoring the intervention. Hard drug use at 12 months or longer: No difference was found (mean difference [MD] -0.01; 95% CI -0.06 to 0.04, based on one study with 1,075 participants, high-quality evidence). Another study without meta-analytic data reported similar results between the intervention and control groups. Any drug use within 12 months: The intervention was associated with a significant reduction in drug use (RR 0.27; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.51, based on two studies with 2,512 participants, moderate-quality evidence). However, one study with 1,566 participants reported no difference in continuous data (MD 0.02; 95% CI -0.05 to 0.09, moderate-quality evidence). Social Influence Approach Marijuana use within 12 months: A near-significant reduction in marijuana use was observed with the social influence approach (RR 0.88; 95% CI 0.72 to 1.07, based on three studies with 10,716 participants, moderate-quality evidence). One study with 764 participants provided continuous data showing a significant effect favoring the intervention (MD -0.26; 95% CI -0.48 to -0.04). Marijuana use at 12 months or longer: No significant difference was found (RR 0.95; 95% CI 0.81 to 1.13, based on one study with 5,862 participants, moderate-quality evidence). Another study with 764 participants showed a near-significant effect favoring the intervention (MD -0.22; 95% CI -0.46 to 0.02). Of four additional studies without meta-analytic data, only one reported a significant protective effect. Hard drug use at 12 months or longer: One study without meta-analytic data reported a significant protective effect of the social influence approach. Any drug use: No studies assessed this outcome. Combined Approach Marijuana use within 12 months: A trend favoring the combined intervention was observed (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.59 to 1.05, based on three studies with 8,701 participants, moderate-quality evidence). One study with 693 participants reported no difference in continuous data (MD -1.90; 95% CI -5.83 to 2.03). Marijuana use at 12 months or longer: The combined intervention showed a protective effect (RR 0.83; 95% CI 0.69 to 0.99, based on six studies with 26,910 participants, moderate-quality evidence). One study with 690 participants reported no difference in continuous data (MD -0.80; 95% CI -4.39 to 2.79). Two additional studies without meta-analytic data found no significant effect. Hard drug use within 12 months: One study with 693 participants provided both dichotomous and continuous data, showing conflicting results. No difference was observed for dichotomous outcomes (RR 0.85; 95% CI 0.63 to 1.14), but continuous data favored the intervention (MD -3.10; 95% CI -5.90 to -0.30, high-quality evidence). Hard drug use at 12 months or longer: No significant difference was found (RR 0.86; 95% CI 0.39 to 1.90, based on two studies with 1,066 participants, high-quality evidence). One study with 690 participants reported no difference in continuous data (MD 0.30; 95% CI -1.36 to 1.96). Two additional studies without meta-analytic data reported significant effects of the intervention. Any drug use within 12 months: The combined intervention was associated with a significant reduction in drug use (RR 0.76; 95% CI 0.64 to 0.89, based on one study with 6,362 participants). Knowledge-Focused Interventions Only one study assessed the effect of a knowledge-focused intervention on drug use and found no significant effect. Authors' Conclusions School-based programs that combine social competence and social influence approaches demonstrated small but consistent protective effects in preventing drug use. Some programs focusing solely on social competence also showed protective effects for certain outcomes. However, given the modest impact of these interventions, they should be integrated into broader, more comprehensive strategies to achieve meaningful population-level reductions in drug use.
